input: what are those fixed boxes in ram called that each hold one chunk of a program's memory?
expected_output: They are called page frames. Physical memory is viewed as an array of fixed-sized slots, and each of these frames can contain a single virtual-memory page.

evidence.quote: Correspondingly, we view physical memory as an array of fixed-sized slots called page frames; each of these frames can contain a single virtual-memory page.

input: what does the os keep around to remember where each piece of a program's memory landed in ram?
expected_output: It keeps a page table, which is usually a per-process data structure. Its major role is to store the address translations for each virtual page of the address space, so the system knows where in physical memory each page resides.

evidence.quote: the operating system usually keeps a per-process data structure known as a page table. The major role of the page table is to store address translations for each of the virtual pages of the address space, thus letting us know where in physical memory each page resides.

input: why isn't the page table just kept in a special spot on the cpu instead of in regular ram?
expected_output: Page tables get very large, so the MMU does not have special on-chip hardware to hold the page table of the currently-running process. Instead, the page table for each process is stored somewhere in memory.

evidence.quote: Because page tables are so big, we don’t keep any special on-chip hardware in the MMU to store the page table of the currently-running process. Instead, we store the page table for each process in memory somewhere.

input: how does a program with a mostly empty giant address space avoid wasting ram on the empty part?
expected_output: The unused space between the code/heap at one end and the stack at the other is marked invalid in the page table via the valid bit. Because those pages are marked invalid, no physical frames need to be allocated for them, which saves a great deal of memory. This is what makes a sparse address space workable.

evidence.quote: Thus, the valid bit is crucial for supporting a sparse address space; by simply marking all the unused pages in the address space invalid, we remove the need to allocate physical frames for those pages and thus save a great deal of memory.
All the unused space in-between will be marked invalid, and if the process tries to access such memory, it will generate a trap to the OS which will likely terminate the process.

A valid bit is common to indicate whether the particular translation is valid; for example, when a program starts running, it will have code and heap at one end of its address space, and the stack at the other.

input: When a virtual address is translated, why is only the upper part replaced while the low-order bits carry over unchanged?
expected_output: The low bits form the offset, which tells us which byte within the page we are interested in. Since the offset only identifies a byte inside the page, it stays the same and is not translated.

evidence.quote: Note the offset stays the same (i.e., it is not translated), because the offset just tells us which byte within the page we want.
The remaining bits tell us which byte of the page we are interested in, 4 bits in this case; we call this the offset.

input: paging makes ram access slower somehow?? like whats the extra work each time
expected_output: With the page table in memory, the hardware must first fetch the proper page-table entry before it can perform the translation and load the data. So every memory reference, whether an instruction fetch or an explicit load or store, needs one extra memory reference to get the translation. That is costly and will likely slow the process by a factor of two or more.

evidence.quote: For every memory reference (whether an instruction fetch or an explicit load or store), paging requires us to perform one extra memory reference in order to first fetch the translation from the page table.
Extra memory references are costly, and in this case will likely slow down the process by a factor of two or more.

Thus, before fetching the data from address 117, the system must first fetch the proper page table entry from the process’s page table, perform the translation, and then load the data from physical memory.

input: how is paging different from segmentation and why does it avoid fragmentation
expected_output: Segmentation splits an address space into variable-sized logical pieces such as code, heap and stack, while paging divides it into fixed-sized units called pages. Dividing space into different-size chunks can leave the space itself fragmented and make allocation harder over time. Paging, by dividing memory into fixed-sized units by design, does not lead to external fragmentation.

evidence.quote: Instead of splitting up a process’s address space into some number of variable-sized logical segments (e.g., code, heap, stack), we divide it into fixed-sized units, each of which we call a page.
In particular, when dividing a space into different-size chunks, the space itself can become fragmented, and thus allocation becomes more challenging over time.
First, it does not lead to external fragmentation, as paging (by design) divides memory into fixed-sized units.

input: whats the difference between the dirty bit and the accessed bit in a pte
expected_output: The dirty bit says whether the page has been modified since it was brought into memory. The reference (accessed) bit tracks whether the page has been accessed at all, and is useful for deciding which pages are popular and should stay in memory.

evidence.quote: A dirty bit is also common, indicating whether the page has been modified since it was brought into memory.
A reference bit (a.k.a. accessed bit) is sometimes used to track whether a page has been accessed, and is useful in determining which pages are popular and thus should be kept in memory

input: say i have a 256 byte address space with 32 byte pages, virtual address 100 is in frame 6, whats the physical address
expected_output: Split the address into a virtual page number and an offset. With 32-byte pages the offset is 5 bits and the VPN is the top 3 bits of the 8-bit address: 100 = 011 00100, so VPN 3 and offset 4. Replace the VPN with the PFN (6) and keep the offset: 6*32 + 4 = 196.

evidence.quote: To translate this virtual address that the process generated, we have to first split it into two components: the virtual page number (VPN), and the offset within the page.
Thus, we can translate this virtual address by replacing the VPN with the PFN and then issue the load to physical memory (Figure 18.3).

expected_output: 1KB pages need 10 offset bits, leaving a 22-bit VPN, so each process has 2^22 (about 4 million) translations. At 4 bytes each that is 16MB per page table. Since every process has its own table, 10 processes need about 160MB.

input: in the translation code what are the mask and the shift for, like why do an & and then a >>
expected_output: The VPN mask picks out just the VPN bits from the full virtual address. The shift is set to the number of bits in the offset, so it moves those VPN bits down to form the correct integer virtual page number, which is then used as the index into the page table.

evidence.quote: VPN MASK would be set to 0x30 (hex 30, or binary 110000) which picks out the VPN bits from the full virtual address; SHIFT is set to 4 (the number of bits in the offset), such that we move the VPN bits down to form the correct integer virtual page number.

input: since every process starts its addresses at 0 anyway, the os only needs one big translation table that everyone shares, right?
expected_output: No. The page table is a per-process data structure, so each process gets its own. If another process runs, the OS has to manage a different page table for it, because its virtual pages map to different physical pages (apart from any sharing).

evidence.quote: It is important to remember that this page table is a per-process data structure

If another process were to run in our example above, the OS would have to manage a different page table for it, as its virtual pages obviously map to different physical pages (modulo any sharing going on).

input: the valid bit in a pte is what says whether the page is in ram or got swapped out to disk, right?
expected_output: No, that is the job of the present bit, which indicates whether the page is in physical memory or on disk. The valid bit instead says whether the translation itself is valid; for instance, the unused space between the code/heap and the stack is marked invalid.

evidence.quote: A present bit indicates whether this page is in physical memory or on disk (i.e., it has been swapped out).

A valid bit is common to indicate whether the particular translation is valid; for example, when a program starts running, it will have code and heap at one end of its address space, and the stack at the other.
All the unused space in-between will be marked invalid, and if the process tries to access such memory, it will generate a trap to the OS which will likely terminate the process.

input: A loop body has 3 instructions and one of them writes to an array element. With paging, how many memory references happen per iteration and why?
expected_output: Each instruction fetch produces two memory references: one to the page table to find the frame the instruction lives in, and one to fetch the instruction itself. That is 3 x 2 = 6. The array write adds one more page-table access to translate the array address and then the array access itself, for 2 more, so 8 per iteration.

evidence.quote: each instruction fetch will generate two memory references: one to the page table to find the physical frame that the instruction resides within, and one to the instruction itself to fetch it to the CPU for processing.

In addition, there is one explicit memory reference in the form of the mov instruction; this adds another page table access first (to translate the array virtual address to the correct physical one) and then the array access itself.
